title: Can turning a transversal make corresponding angles equal?
description: Two lines lean ten degrees apart, so they are not parallel. The board turns a transversal and finds that the two corresponding angles always differ by ten degrees. Keeko doubts that a big enough turn makes them match.
teaching_notes: One idea: for lines that are not parallel, the corresponding angles stay a fixed amount apart however the transversal turns. Watch for students who think a big enough turn will make them match.

source: Two lines l and m lean 10° apart, so they are not parallel. A transversal t makes 30° with l, and m leans 10° more towards t than l does, so t makes 20° with m on the matching side. Can the two corresponding angles be made equal by turning t?
video_script.why: The child sees why corresponding angles of lines that are not parallel can never be equal.
video_script.substitution: The book's own activity: draw a transversal to two lines that are not parallel and try to make a pair of corresponding angles equal.
video_script.anchor: Two lines l and m leaning ten degrees apart and a transversal t, with the two corresponding angles marked.
video_script.wrong_answer: turn it far enough and they match
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a big enough turn of the transversal makes the angles match.
video_script.payoff_line: No, the corresponding angles always differ by ten degrees.

final_answer.value: No; the corresponding angles always differ by 10°
final_answer.spoken: no, the corresponding angles always differ by ten degrees

hold_back: No; the corresponding angles always differ by 10°
maths_rules: the corresponding angles are 30 and 20, and 30 - 20 = 10
turn t to make 50 with l; then it makes 40 with m, and 50 - 40 = 10
each time the two angles differ by 10, because the lines lean 10 degrees apart
so no transversal makes them equal: corresponding angles of lines that are not parallel are never equal
the slip: turning t changes both angles by the same amount, so the gap between them stays
video_script.design: One figure stays on the stage. The transversal turns once, the two angles are marked before and after, and the difference is written each time.
